clinicalPearls: Cement causes two overlapping problems: an irritant contact dermatitis from its strong alkalinity, abrasive particles and hygroscopic drying effect, and an allergic contact dermatitis, chiefly to hexavalent chromium and cobalt.
Wet cement is highly alkaline and can produce not only eczema but full-thickness alkaline (caustic) burns, classically on the knees, feet and lower legs of kneeling concrete workers.
Chromate is the dominant allergen in cement dermatitis; adding ferrous sulfate to reduce hexavalent to trivalent chromium has markedly lowered the incidence where mandated.
The eruption typically affects the hands, wrists and forearms, and any skin in prolonged contact with wet concrete through clothing or boots.
Allergic cement dermatitis tends to be chronic and persistent, often continuing despite avoidance because of the ubiquity of chromate and the entrenched sensitisation.
A history of an itchy hand eczema that flares at work and settles on holiday, in a construction or masonry worker, is highly suggestive.
Patch testing to potassium dichromate and cobalt chloride confirms the allergic component and guides prognosis and workplace advice.
Prevention relies on low-chromate (ferrous-sulfate-treated) cement, waterproof protective clothing and gloves, prompt washing of skin contamination and avoiding kneeling in wet concrete.
reference.pathophysiology: Cement injures skin by several mechanisms. Its high alkalinity (calcium hydroxide and related species when hydrated) saponifies lipids and denatures keratin, producing irritant dermatitis and, with prolonged contact, alkaline caustic burns; the abrasive mineral particles and desiccating properties add mechanical and drying injury that further disrupts the barrier. Superimposed on this is allergic contact dermatitis: hexavalent chromium and cobalt present as soluble contaminants penetrate the compromised epidermis, bind proteins to form haptens and elicit a delayed (type IV) T-cell-mediated hypersensitivity, giving a chronic spongiotic eczema. Barrier damage from the irritant effects enhances allergen penetration and perpetuates sensitisation, so the two processes reinforce each other. Reducing hexavalent to trivalent chromium (for example with added ferrous sulfate) lowers the allergenic load and the risk of new sensitisation.

redFlags: deep or extensive alkaline burns from prolonged wet-cement contact
circumferential or full-thickness skin loss requiring surgical assessment
severe secondarily infected eczema with systemic features
persistent disabling dermatitis threatening the worker's livelihood
signs of concurrent chromate exposure such as nasal septal ulceration
reference.prognosis: Irritant cement dermatitis often improves with barrier protection and good skin care, but allergic (chromate) cement dermatitis is frequently chronic and may persist even after leaving the trade because of established sensitisation and ubiquitous exposure. Alkaline burns can cause significant scarring.
pitfalls: Assuming all cement dermatitis is irritant and omitting patch testing for chromate and cobalt.
Underestimating wet cement as a cause of serious alkaline burns, especially on the knees.
Expecting resolution on avoidance and failing to warn of the chronicity of chromate allergy.
Relying on ordinary gloves that are permeable to wet cement or fail with prolonged contact.
Overlooking coexisting rubber-glove allergy contributing to hand eczema.
references: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, current edition
Adams' Occupational Skin Disease, current edition
management: Allergen and irritant avoidance, using chromate-reduced cement in which ferrous sulfate converts hexavalent to trivalent chromium
Protective measures with impermeable gloves, protective clothing and barrier creams to prevent contact with wet cement
Topical corticosteroids to settle acute eczema, with emollients to restore the skin barrier
Prompt copious irrigation and wound care of alkaline caustic burns, classically over the knees and lower legs
Antibiotics for secondary bacterial infection where present
Patch testing to potassium dichromate and cobalt to confirm the allergy and guide avoidance

Occupational health review with workplace modification and, for persistent allergic disease, consideration of a change of trade, with patient education that sensitisation may persist despite avoidance
